newsitem.title: USA: Louisiana Senate race not over, Republican says.
newsitem.headline: Louisiana Senate race not over, Republican says.

text.p: Republican Woody Jenkins, who trailed Democrat Mary Landrieu by only 7,629 votes in unofficial counts of Louisiana's heated U.S. Senate race, said early Wednesday that the election was not over yet.

Calling the election "probably the closest in Louisiana history," Jenkins said after Landrieu was named the unofficial victor that the numbers could change Friday when voting machines are opened and absentee ballots recounted.

"When you go through this process there are always many errors ... mostly innocent transpositions of numbers. We know that only two votes per precinct could change this election," Jenkins said. He also said his campaign would look at "any possible election irregularities that may have occurred."

Wade Martin, head of the Louisiana Secretary of State's elections division, told Reuters on Wednesday there were fewer claims of irregularities than usual in an election this size. More than 1.7 million residents voted on Tuesday.

Barring a court challenge, the election results will be final on Nov. 21. One congressional election 20 years ago was so fraught with irregularities that the courts ordered a new election. Other election night results with wider margins of victory have changed when ballots were recounted.

Landrieu, a Catholic who backs a woman's right to have an abortion, claimed victory early Wednesday after 100 percent of the unofficial returns were announced. Local and national television called it in her favour almost two hours earlier.
If her lead holds, she will become the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate from Louisiana. If Jenkins goes ahead, he would be the state's first Republican senator in a century.

Political analysts said Landrieu profited far more from multi-million-dollar "get out the vote" drives launched by gambling advocates for local option gambling initiatives on the ballots than from all the whistle-stop campaigning by President Clinton and other prominent Democrats.
"Voters in the parishes where riverboats are docked turned out in high numbers to support the boats and carried Landrieu with them," analyst Mike Baer said. Jenkins opposes gambling.
